\chapter{The Sky}
\label{ch:ka-sky}
\hlchaptermodality{53}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five things overhead in Kannada, and say which of them Kannada borrowed and which it has always had.}

Complete KA-C53-cloud and say all five words in order.

\section[ākāśa]{\kn{ಆಕಾಶ} (ākāśa) — the sky}

\label{lesson:KA-C53-sky}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run: what did \emph{hūvu} mean, and what did \emph{hūmāle} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಆಕಾಶ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಆಕಾಶ}} (\emph{ākāśa}) — \textquotedblleft{}the sky\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{ākāśa}, built on a piece meaning \textquotedblleft{}to shine, to be visible\textquotedblright{}. The sky is named for being the open lit place where a thing can be seen at all, rather than for being a lid over the world.

Kannada holds an inherited word for the same overhead space, \kn{ಬಾನು} (\emph{bānu}), which owes Sanskrit nothing. The two divide the work: \kn{ಆಕಾಶ} does the ordinary shift and turns up in weather talk, while \kn{ಬಾನು} keeps to songs and poetry. A borrowed word taking the daily job and leaving the old one the ceremony is an arrangement you have watched before, at the \kn{ಬಾಗಿಲು}.

\emph{ākāśa} travelled as well. Traders carried it east, and Malay and Indonesian still say \emph{angkasa} for the sky.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The space the rest of this chapter hangs in.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ākāśa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ākāśa}, then \emph{namaskāra}, as you would greet somebody out of doors
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಆಕಾಶ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the sky\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bisilu]{\kn{ಬಿಸಿಲು} (bisilu) — sunshine, the sun's heat}

\label{lesson:KA-C53-sunshine}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ākāśa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಬಿಸಿಲು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಬಿಸಿಲು}} (\emph{bisilu}) — \textquotedblleft{}sunshine, the sun's heat\textquotedblright{}.

Under it sits \kn{ಬಿಸಿ} (\emph{bisi}), \textquotedblleft{}hot\textquotedblright{} — the word on a cup of \kn{ಚಹಾ} that has just been poured. \kn{ಬಿಸಿಲು} is the hot thing that falls out of the sky, and Kannada built it the plain way, from the heat rather than from the star.

That is worth pausing on. English talks about the weather by naming the sun; Kannada reaches first for what the sun does to you standing in it. A Bengaluru sentence about the afternoon is far more likely to be about \kn{ಬಿಸಿಲು} than about any sun-word at all.

Kannada has two sun-words even so. \kn{ನೇಸರು} (\emph{nēsaru}) is its own, kept alive mostly in verse and in names; the borrowed one you have already had a piece of, inside the sunrise word the good-morning lesson took apart.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: the sky, and what comes down out of it by day.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bisilu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bisi}, then \emph{bisilu}, and hear the shorter word standing inside the longer one
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಬಿಸಿಲು} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}sunshine, the sun's heat\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[candra]{\kn{ಚಂದ್ರ} (candra) — the moon}

\label{lesson:KA-C53-moon}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bisilu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಚಂದ್ರ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಚಂದ್ರ}} (\emph{candra}) — \textquotedblleft{}the moon\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{candra} means \textquotedblleft{}shining, bright\textquotedblright{}. Kannada took it whole, the way it took \kn{ಆಕಾಶ}, and it is the word a newsreader says.

Kannada's own moon-word is \kn{ತಿಂಗಳು} (\emph{tiṅgaḷu}), and that word also means a month. One shape for the moon and for the stretch of time it measures — the moon being the oldest calendar there is, and Kannada keeping that fact inside a single word. The twelve month-names you met are Sanskrit; \kn{ತಿಂಗಳು} is what a Kannada speaker actually counts in.

\emph{candra} went a long way west too. It shares an ancestor with the Latin piece behind English \emph{candle} and \emph{incandescent}: a very old root for burning white.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and two of them borrowed.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{candra}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ākāśa}, then \emph{candra}, and say which of the two is the container
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಚಂದ್ರ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the moon\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cukki]{\kn{ಚುಕ್ಕಿ} (cukki) — a star; a dot}

\label{lesson:KA-C53-star}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{candra} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಚುಕ್ಕಿ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಚುಕ್ಕಿ}} (\emph{cukki}) — \textquotedblleft{}a star; a dot\textquotedblright{}.

\kn{ಚುಕ್ಕಿ} is inherited, and it carries the star and the dot on one shape. Anything small and round and separate can be a \kn{ಚುಕ್ಕಿ}.

Which is why it belongs to the \kn{ರಂಗೋಲಿ} as much as to the night. The pattern at the doorway is set out first as a grid of \kn{ಚುಕ್ಕಿ}, points of rice flour placed at even spacing, and the lines are drawn around and between them afterwards. A woman saying she is putting down \kn{ಚುಕ್ಕಿ} in the morning is talking about her doorstep.

The borrowed word for a star is \kn{ನಕ್ಷತ್ರ} (\emph{nakṣatra}), and that is the one an astrologer reaches for. \kn{ಚುಕ್ಕಿ} is the one a child points with.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and this one reaches back down to the doorstep.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cukki}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{cukki}, then \emph{raṅgōli}, and say how the two meet on the ground
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಚುಕ್ಕಿ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a star; a dot\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mōḍa]{\kn{ಮೋಡ} (mōḍa) — a cloud}

\label{lesson:KA-C53-cloud}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{cukki} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಮೋಡ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಮೋಡ}} (\emph{mōḍa}) — \textquotedblleft{}a cloud\textquotedblright{}.

\kn{ಮೋಡ} is inherited and quite plain: the grey thing standing between you and the \kn{ಬಿಸಿಲು}. \kn{ಮೋಡ} \kn{ಇದೆ} — there is cloud — is a whole weather report, and it is the one Kannada speakers give each other most of the year.

Weather words stretch, and this one has. \kn{ಮೋಡ} also describes a face that has gone dull and closed, and a mood that will not lift. English went the same way with \emph{clouded} and \emph{overcast}, from the far side of the world and with no contact at all. When two unrelated languages reach for the same picture, the picture is doing the work rather than any borrowing.

With that, the sky is furnished.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \kn{ಆಕಾಶ}, \kn{ಬಿಸಿಲು}, \kn{ಚಂದ್ರ}, \kn{ಚುಕ್ಕಿ}, \kn{ಮೋಡ}. You can say what is overhead.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then say which two of them Kannada borrowed
\end{itemize}
